items.title: The Domesday Book recorded almost every pig in England
items.claim: William I commissioned the Domesday survey in 1085, completed 1086. How detailed was it?

options.text: It listed only the major landholders and royal manors
It recorded landholders, ploughs, mills, fishponds, livestock and even individual peasants down to the level of swineherds — over 13,000 places
It was a list of military obligations only

items.reveal_title: Not one ox or cow escaped
items.reveal:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (E text) complained: 'So very narrowly did he have it investigated that there was no single hide nor a yard of land, nor indeed (it is a shame to relate but it seemed no shame to him to do) one ox nor one cow nor one pig which was left out.'

Commissioners visited every shire, took sworn testimony, and produced the survey in around a year. The original manuscripts (Great Domesday and Little Domesday) survive at The National Archives, Kew.
items.why: Medieval government is often dismissed as primitive. Domesday is more administratively detailed than anything attempted in Europe for centuries afterwards.

items.title: Nobody called it the Wars of the Roses at the time
items.claim: The wars between Lancaster and York (1455-1487) are remembered for the red and white rose badges. What is the actual history of those symbols?

options.text: Both sides wore rose badges throughout the conflict
The white rose was a Yorkist badge, but the red Lancastrian rose was largely a Tudor-era invention — Henry VII used the union of the roses as propaganda
The roses came from heraldic tradition dating to the Conquest
The name was coined in 1485 by Henry VII himself

items.reveal_title: The Tudor rose was the spin
items.reveal:
Edward IV used a white rose among other badges. The red rose was a minor Lancastrian badge under Henry IV but rarely used during the wars themselves. The 'Tudor rose' (red and white combined) was created after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486 — the union as legitimising symbol.

The name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularised by Walter Scott's novel 'Anne of Geierstein' (1829). Shakespeare's 'Henry VI Part 1' invented the Temple Garden scene where nobles pluck the rival roses.
items.why: Historical memory is shaped by later spin. The Tudor regime had every reason to dramatise dynastic union; Shakespeare amplified the imagery; Scott named it. Almost none of that was visible in 1460.

items.title: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991

options.text: After Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost reforms, the August 1991 hardline coup failed, Baltic states declared independence, Yeltsin took power in Russia; the USSR was formally dissolved by the Belavezha Accords (8 December) and Gorbachev's resignation (25 December); the Supreme Soviet voted itself out of existence on 26 December 1991
By a vote of all citizens in 1989

items.reveal:
Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary in March 1985. Perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness) loosened Soviet controls. Eastern European communism collapsed in 1989. The Baltic states declared independence in 1990-91.

The August 1991 coup by hardliners against Gorbachev failed within three days when Boris Yeltsin rallied resistance from a tank outside the Russian White House. Real power shifted from the USSR to Russia.

The Belavezha Accords (8 December 1991) saw the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declare the USSR dissolved. The Alma-Ata Protocol (21 December) added eight more republics. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December; the Supreme Soviet voted on 26 December.
items.why: The largest peaceful end of a superpower in history. The mechanism — internal reform, failed counter-coup, voluntary dissolution by republics — has shaped how subsequent transitions have been imagined.
